## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The retrieved record confirms the ingredient as **sertraline**. LactMed is lactation-specific and does not provide pregnancy evidence. [S9](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Measured milk and infant exposure

- LactMed reports generally low sertraline concentrations in breast milk. The metabolite **norsertraline** was often detectable at low levels in infant serum. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In reported studies, infant serum sertraline was frequently undetectable, although some infants had measurable sertraline and/or norsertraline. Exposure estimates varied with sampling timing, breastfeeding extent, and study population. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One report involved a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks** with measured sertraline and norsertraline in serum. The record also describes genetically intermediate metabolism; the retrieved evidence does not establish that sertraline caused the reported symptoms. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are measured exposure findings, not clinical outcomes by themselves.

### Observed infant outcomes

- Several small observational groups reported no observed acute adverse effects, and one group reported normal infant weight gain through 6 months. The retrieved LactMed metadata does not establish a study count; missing study counts are unknown, not zero. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed reports one 4-month-old infant with benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. The source does not establish causation. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In the preterm-infant report, symptoms described as similar to neonatal abstinence occurred in the context of prematurity and genetically intermediate metabolism. The returned extract is insufficient to determine the causal contribution of sertraline. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed’s summary reports no developmental adverse effects in infants followed for up to 5 years in the cited material, but this does not establish safety for every infant or circumstance. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Completeness limitation:** The retrieved LactMed “Effects in Breastfed Infants” section is truncated, and “Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk” was omitted by the retrieval limit. This is not a complete LactMed record. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

## Product-label evidence

The selected DailyMed product is **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, with an effective date of November 5, 2026. The exact product and formulation match was not confirmed. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The retrieved label’s adverse-reactions section describes findings in the **medicine-taking label population**, not breastfed infants. It lists hypersensitivity, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, activation of mania/hypomania, seizures, hyponatremia, sexual dysfunction, and other product-label concerns. These are not observed infant outcomes. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The retrieved label extract did not include the expected warnings, boxed-warning, warnings-and-precautions, or drug-interactions sections. Their absence from this extract does not prove that the product’s full labeling lacks those sections. DailyMed also notes that in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

## Questions to ask a clinician

- Does the selected label match the exact product and formulation?
- How closely does the evidence match the infant’s age, prematurity status, health conditions, and extent of breastfeeding?
- Which findings are measured exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- What uncertainty remains because the LactMed extract is truncated?
- What parent and infant follow-up is appropriate in this situation?
- How should the benefits of treating the parent’s underlying condition and the risks of medication changes be considered together?

Stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and belongs in a discussion with the prescribing clinician.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

breastfeeding_evidence.title: Sertraline
breastfeeding_evidence.text:
Summary of Use during Lactation: Because of the low levels of sertraline in breastmilk, amounts ingested by the infant are small and is usually not detected in the serum of the infant, although the weakly active metabolite norsertraline (desmethylsertraline) is often detectable in low levels in infant serum. Rarely, preterm infants with impaired metabolic activity might accumulate the drug and demonstrate symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence. No adverse effects on development have been found in infants followed for up to 5 years of age. Most authoritative reviewers consider sertraline a preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.[1-9] Mothers taking an SSRI during pregnancy and postpartum may have more difficulty breastfeeding, although this might be a reflection of their disease state.[10] These mothers may need additional breastfeeding support. Breastfed infants exposed to an SSRI during the third trimester of pregnancy are at risk for neonatal withdrawal syndrome consisting of hypoglycemia, tremors, tachycardia, or hypotonia, and might be at a greater risk of readmission due to jaundice.[11,12]

Drug Levels: Sertraline is metabolized to norsertraline (desmethylsertraline), which has antidepressant activity of about 10% that of sertraline. Maternal Levels. In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 4 unpublished cases, the authors found that 15 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 83 mg (range 25 to 200 mg) had an average breastmilk sertraline level of 45 mcg/L (range 7 to 207 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of sertraline. Twenty-six women who were an average of 15.8 weeks postpartum (range 5 to 36 weeks) and receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied while breastfeeding with extensive milk and serum sampling over a 24-hour period. All milk samples had detectable sertraline (average 129 mcg/L; range 11 to 938 mcg/L) and norsertraline (average 258 mcg/L; range 20 to 1498 mcg/L). Drug concentrations were higher in the hindmilk than the foremilk. Analysis of milk sertraline data from 15 mothers who submitted complete sets of milk samples indicated that the peak concentration of the drug and metabolite occurred 8 to 9 hours after a dose. In these women, the concentration in milk correlated with serum concentration, but not daily dosage. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an average of 0.54% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage and that pumping and discarding milk 8 to 9 hours after the mother’s dose would decrease the infant’s daily dosage by 17%.[13] From data in 6 mothers who were 5 to 34 weeks postpartum and taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 64 mg (range 50 to 100 mg), the authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.9% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[14] At 2 months postpartum, 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had average milk levels of 26.4 mcg/L of sertraline and 29 mcg/L of norsertraline at random times after the previous dose. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.04 mg/kg of sertraline daily.[15] The mother of a preterm infant was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during pregnancy and postpartum. Her breastmilk levels of sertraline and norsertraline on 3 days at random times averaged 201 and 358 mcg/L, respectively.[16] One woman taking sertraline 25 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 29 mcg/L at two times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 4.4 mcg/kg daily or 0.6% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage. In the same paper, 3 women taking sertraline 50 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 58 mcg/L at times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 8.7 mcg/kg daily or 1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[17] A nursing mother was taking sertraline 50 mg daily. Foremilk and hindmilk samples taken at 4 weeks postpartum, 13 hours after a dose contained 26 mcg/L and 46 mcg/L, respectively.[18] Nine women treated with sertraline 25 to 75 mg daily (7 were taking 50 mg daily) during the third trimester of pregnancy and during breastfeeding provided trough milk samples during the first week postpartum. Sertraline was undetectable (<5 mcg/L) in the milk of 1 woman taking 50 mg daily. In the other 8 women, milk levels ranged from 11.1 to 24.5 mcg/L, with calculated weight-adjusted percentage of maternal dosages ranging from 0.2 to 2.4%. These values might be inaccurate because of the timing of milk sample collection.[19] Random milk samples were obtained from 6 women taking a median dosage of 50 mg (range 25 to 50 mg) of sertraline daily had a median sertraline milk concentration of 11.3 mcg/L (range 3.6 to 35.7 mcg/L). The authors calculated that this represents a median infant dosage of 1.6 (range 0.5 to 5.4) mcg/kg daily. No correlation was found between maternal dosage and milk sertraline level.[20] Fifteen mothers taking sertraline in an average dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) provided milk samples for analysis. Samples of milk from the complete emptying of one breast were collected 3 times over a 2-day period at predefined times between just before a dose and 14 hours after a dose, with each participant collecting samples at different times. The average milk concentration was 87 mcg/L (range 12 to 288 mcg/L) resulting in an average infant daily dosage of 10 mcg/kg and a relative infant dosage of 1%.[21] Thirty-eight mothers taking sertraline with a median daily dose of 50 mg (range 25 to 150 mg) provided 35 blood samples at week 1 postpartum, and 20 at weeks 4 to 6 postpartum. These women also provided 107 breast milk samples, 67 of which were collected at week 1 and 40 at week 4 postpartum. One maternal blood sample was collected and paired with a foremilk and a hindmilk sample. The lower limit of quantification for sertraline was established at 1 mcg/L in plasma and 5 mcg/L in breast milk. These data were used to create a population pharmacokinetic model using NONMEM, which was then used to simulate serum and milk levels in 2000 patients. Simulations suggested a median daily infant dosage of 6.9 mcg/kg with a 50 mg maternal daily dose, representing a relative infant dose of 0.95% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose. The authors found that 100% of simulated infants at maternal doses of 150 mg daily would ingest less than 0.13 mg/kg daily of sertraline, which represents a total of less than 150 mg over 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding.[22] The measurement of fat content in the study may not have been accurate.[23] A woman taking sertraline 100 mg daily provided 5 milk samples between 3.1 and 5.2 days postpartum. Sertraline concentrations ranged from 53.4 mcg/L at 6 hours after a dose to 15.5 mcg/L at 24 hours after a dose.[24] Infant Levels. A paper reported 3 breastfed infants whose mother were taking sertraline. A woman taking 50 mg daily increased her dose to 75 mg daily after 2 weeks. Sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<2 mg/L) in her 4-week-old infant’s serum. Another infant whose mother was taking 75 mg daily which was increased to 100 mg daily had detectable norsertraline (<2 mg/L), but no sertraline (<1 mg/L). A third woman taking 75 mg daily found no detectable sertraline or norsertraline in her infant’s serum at 8 weeks of age. The extent of nursing was not reported in any of the cases.[25] Of 30 breastfed infants (19 exclusively, 11 breastfed 50% or more) aged 6 to 13 weeks, 22 had undetectable (<1 mcg/L) sertraline serum levels during maternal therapy with sertraline dosages of 25 to 200 mg daily. Of the 8 infants who had detectable serum levels, their average sertraline serum level was 7.9 mcg/L. Their mothers, who were taking an average of 109 mg daily, had an average serum level of 52.8 mcg/L.[26] In a pooled analysis of 53 mother-infant pairs from published and unpublished cases, the authors found that infants had an average of 2% (range 0 to 15%) of the sertraline plasma concentrations of the mothers’; 3 of the infants had a plasma level greater than 10% of the mothers’, which was considered by the authors as being elevated.[1] Twenty-two breastfed (20 exclusively) infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied. Infant serum levels were measured 2.2 hours (range 0.5 to 5 hours) after nursing. Four infants had detectable sertraline (>2 mcg/L) and 11 infants had detectable norsertraline in their serum with an average concentration of 22 mcg/L. One 11-week-old infant who was being treated for acute asthma with albuterol, inhaled corticosteroids and hydroxyzine had serum levels higher than its mother’s, even though 4 other infants received higher doses of sertraline and norsertraline through milk.[13] In 6 breastfed (extent not stated) infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 15 mg (range 5 to 34 mg), sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<3.4 mcg/L).[14] In a study of mothers given sertraline prophylactically for recurrent postpartum depression, 7 opted to breastfeed. Infant serum was tested at 4 weeks of age with a maternal dosage of 50 mg daily. Sertraline (<2 mcg/L) and norsertraline (<12 mcg/L) were undetectable in the serum of any infant.[27] In a study comparing sertraline to nortriptyline for postpartum depression, 13 infants were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline (dosage and extent of nursing were not stated). After a constant maternal sertraline dosage for at least 14 days, infants had their serum concentrations measured. The infants were an average of 5.9 weeks old at the time of serum sampling. Sertraline was not detectable (<2 mcg/L) in any of the infants’ serum; norsertraline serum levels ranged from undetectable (<2 mcg/L) to 6 mcg/L.[28] At 2 months postpartum, the breastfed infants of 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had undetectable (<0.1 mcg/L) serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline.[15] A 33-week preterm infant was exclusively breastfed by a mother who was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during gestation, at delivery and postpartum. Because of symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence syndrome, the infant’s serum concentrations of sertraline and desmethylsertraline were measured on day 5 postpartum. Levels were 13 and 52 mcg/L, respectively. Because of ongoing symptoms, breastfeeding was stopped on day 9 and the infant’s serum levels reportedly dropped, although specific values were not presented in the paper. The infant was later found to have genetically intermediate metabolism of two of the CYP450 enzymes involved in sertraline metabolism.[16] Authors of a meta-analysis on sertraline reported infant serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline in 25 infants who were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline. Ten of the infants were exclusively breastfed, two were 80% breastfed and the breastfeeding status of the others was not reported. Only two infants, both exclusively breastfed, had detectable serum sertraline levels of 2.1 and 2.4 mcg/L. The other infants had undetectable (<2 mcg/L) sertraline levels. Four other infants had detectable norsertraline levels ranging from 2.6 to 4.7 mcg/L. Sampling times were not reported.[6] Fifteen breastfed (extent not stated) infants with an average age of 1.4 months (range 1.0 to 2.6 months) whose mothers were taking an average sertraline dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) had one blood sample taken for analysis. Their average serum level of sertraline was <2 mcg/L (range <2 to 2.6 mcg/L).[21]

Effects in Breastfed Infants: Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus occurred in one 4-month-old infant and agitation that spontaneously resolved whose mother was taking sertraline 75 mg daily.[25] None of 26 infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily had any detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk. All had been breastfeeding for at least 3 weeks.[13] Whole blood serotonin levels were measured in 14 mothers and their breastfed infants after 6 to 16 weeks of sertraline therapy. Maternal dosages ranged from 25 to 200 mg daily. Although maternal serotonin levels were decreased from 159 mcg/L to 19 mcg/L by sertraline therapy, infant serotonin levels averaged 227 mcg/L before and 224 mcg/L after maternal therapy. The authors concluded that these findings indicate that the amount of sertraline ingested by the infants was not sufficient to affect platelet serotonin uptake in breastfed infants. Platelets and neurons both have the same serotonin transporter, so this lack of effect was seen as indirect evidence of safety of sertraline use during breastfeeding. None of the infants experienced any adverse effects from sertraline in breastmilk, including 6 exclusively breastfed infants under 3 months of age.[29] Twenty-five mothers who took an average sertraline dosage of 82.4 mg daily breastfed their infants exclusively for 4 months and breastfed at least 50% during months 5 and 6. Their infants had 6-month weight gains that were normal according to national growth standards and the mothers reported no abnormal effects in their infants.[30] In 6 infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline 50 to 100 mg daily, no adverse reactions were noted clinically at the time of the study.[14] No adverse effects were seen in 7 infants who were 4 weeks old and whose mothers had been taking sertraline 50 mg daily since day 4 postpartum.[27] One study of side effects of SSRI antidepressants in nursing mothers found no adverse reactions that required medical attention among 2 infants whose mother was taking sertraline. No specific information on maternal sertraline dosage, extent of breastfeeding or infant age was reported.[31] A small study compared the reaction to pain in infants of depressed mothers who had taken an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and nursing, to a control group of unexposed infants of nondepressed mothers. Infants exposed to an SSRI either prenatally alone or prenatally and postnatally via breastmilk had blunted responses to pain compared to control infants. Four of the 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. Because there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, an effect due to maternal behavior caused by depression could not be ruled out. The authors stressed that these findings did not warrant avoiding drug treatment of depression during pregnancy or avoiding breastfeeding during SSRI treatment.[15] An uncontrolled online survey compiled data on 930 mothers who nursed their infants while taking an antidepressant. Infant drug discontinuation symptoms (e.g., irritability, low body temperature, uncontrollable crying, eating and sleeping disorders) were reported in about 10% of infants. Mothers who took antidepressants only during breastfeeding were much less likely to notice symptoms of drug discontinuation in their infants than those who took the drug in pregnancy and lactation.[32] In a telephone follow-up study, 124 mothers who took a benzodiazepine while nursing reported whether their infants had any signs of sedation. One mother who was taking sertraline 50 mg daily, zopiclone 2.5 mg about every 3 days as needed, and also took alprazolam 0.25 mg on 2 occasions, reported sedation in her breastfed infant.[33] A mother was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during gestation, at delivery and postpartum while exclusively breastfeeding her infant. It works by increasing the amounts of serotonin, a natural substance in the brain that helps maintain mental balance.

breastfeeding_evidence.title: Sertraline
breastfeeding_evidence.text:
Summary of Use during Lactation: Because of the low levels of sertraline in breastmilk, amounts ingested by the infant are small and is usually not detected in the serum of the infant, although the weakly active metabolite norsertraline (desmethylsertraline) is often detectable in low levels in infant serum. Rarely, preterm infants with impaired metabolic activity might accumulate the drug and demonstrate symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence. No adverse effects on development have been found in infants followed for up to 5 years of age. Most authoritative reviewers consider sertraline a preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.[1-9] Mothers taking an SSRI during pregnancy and postpartum may have more difficulty breastfeeding, although this might be a reflection of their disease state.[10] These mothers may need additional breastfeeding support. Breastfed infants exposed to an SSRI during the third trimester of pregnancy are at risk for neonatal withdrawal syndrome consisting of hypoglycemia, tremors, tachycardia, or hypotonia, and might be at a greater risk of readmission due to jaundice.[11,12]

Drug Levels: Sertraline is metabolized to norsertraline (desmethylsertraline), which has antidepressant activity of about 10% that of sertraline. Maternal Levels. In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 4 unpublished cases, the authors found that 15 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 83 mg (range 25 to 200 mg) had an average breastmilk sertraline level of 45 mcg/L (range 7 to 207 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of sertraline. Twenty-six women who were an average of 15.8 weeks postpartum (range 5 to 36 weeks) and receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied while breastfeeding with extensive milk and serum sampling over a 24-hour period. All milk samples had detectable sertraline (average 129 mcg/L; range 11 to 938 mcg/L) and norsertraline (average 258 mcg/L; range 20 to 1498 mcg/L). Drug concentrations were higher in the hindmilk than the foremilk. Analysis of milk sertraline data from 15 mothers who submitted complete sets of milk samples indicated that the peak concentration of the drug and metabolite occurred 8 to 9 hours after a dose. In these women, the concentration in milk correlated with serum concentration, but not daily dosage. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an average of 0.54% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage and that pumping and discarding milk 8 to 9 hours after the mother’s dose would decrease the infant’s daily dosage by 17%.[13] From data in 6 mothers who were 5 to 34 weeks postpartum and taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 64 mg (range 50 to 100 mg), the authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.9% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[14] At 2 months postpartum, 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had average milk levels of 26.4 mcg/L of sertraline and 29 mcg/L of norsertraline at random times after the previous dose. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.04 mg/kg of sertraline daily.[15] The mother of a preterm infant was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during pregnancy and postpartum. Her breastmilk levels of sertraline and norsertraline on 3 days at random times averaged 201 and 358 mcg/L, respectively.[16] One woman taking sertraline 25 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 29 mcg/L at two times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 4.4 mcg/kg daily or 0.6% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage. In the same paper, 3 women taking sertraline 50 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 58 mcg/L at times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 8.7 mcg/kg daily or 1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[17] A nursing mother was taking sertraline 50 mg daily. Foremilk and hindmilk samples taken at 4 weeks postpartum, 13 hours after a dose contained 26 mcg/L and 46 mcg/L, respectively.[18] Nine women treated with sertraline 25 to 75 mg daily (7 were taking 50 mg daily) during the third trimester of pregnancy and during breastfeeding provided trough milk samples during the first week postpartum. Sertraline was undetectable (<5 mcg/L) in the milk of 1 woman taking 50 mg daily. In the other 8 women, milk levels ranged from 11.1 to 24.5 mcg/L, with calculated weight-adjusted percentage of maternal dosages ranging from 0.2 to 2.4%. These values might be inaccurate because of the timing of milk sample collection.[19] Random milk samples were obtained from 6 women taking a median dosage of 50 mg (range 25 to 50 mg) of sertraline daily had a median sertraline milk concentration of 11.3 mcg/L (range 3.6 to 35.7 mcg/L). The authors calculated that this represents a median infant dosage of 1.6 (range 0.5 to 5.4) mcg/kg daily. No correlation was found between maternal dosage and milk sertraline level.[20] Fifteen mothers taking sertraline in an average dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) provided milk samples for analysis. Samples of milk from the complete emptying of one breast were collected 3 times over a 2-day period at predefined times between just before a dose and 14 hours after a dose, with each participant collecting samples at different times. The average milk concentration was 87 mcg/L (range 12 to 288 mcg/L) resulting in an average infant daily dosage of 10 mcg/kg and a relative infant dosage of 1%.[21] Thirty-eight mothers taking sertraline with a median daily dose of 50 mg (range 25 to 150 mg) provided 35 blood samples at week 1 postpartum, and 20 at weeks 4 to 6 postpartum. These women also provided 107 breast milk samples, 67 of which were collected at week 1 and 40 at week 4 postpartum. One maternal blood sample was collected and paired with a foremilk and a hindmilk sample. The lower limit of quantification for sertraline was established at 1 mcg/L in plasma and 5 mcg/L in breast milk. These data were used to create a population pharmacokinetic model using NONMEM, which was then used to simulate serum and milk levels in 2000 patients. Simulations suggested a median daily infant dosage of 6.9 mcg/kg with a 50 mg maternal daily dose, representing a relative infant dose of 0.95% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose. The authors found that 100% of simulated infants at maternal doses of 150 mg daily would ingest less than 0.13 mg/kg daily of sertraline, which represents a total of less than 150 mg over 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding.[22] The measurement of fat content in the study may not have been accurate.[23] A woman taking sertraline 100 mg daily provided 5 milk samples between 3.1 and 5.2 days postpartum. Sertraline concentrations ranged from 53.4 mcg/L at 6 hours after a dose to 15.5 mcg/L at 24 hours after a dose.[24] Infant Levels. A paper reported 3 breastfed infants whose mother were taking sertraline. A woman taking 50 mg daily increased her dose to 75 mg daily after 2 weeks. Sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<2 mg/L) in her 4-week-old infant’s serum. Another infant whose mother was taking 75 mg daily which was increased to 100 mg daily had detectable norsertraline (<2 mg/L), but no sertraline (<1 mg/L). A third woman taking 75 mg daily found no detectable sertraline or norsertraline in her infant’s serum at 8 weeks of age. The extent of nursing was not reported in any of the cases.[25] Of 30 breastfed infants (19 exclusively, 11 breastfed 50% or more) aged 6 to 13 weeks, 22 had undetectable (<1 mcg/L) sertraline serum levels during maternal therapy with sertraline dosages of 25 to 200 mg daily. Of the 8 infants who had detectable serum levels, their average sertraline serum level was 7.9 mcg/L. Their mothers, who were taking an average of 109 mg daily, had an average serum level of 52.8 mcg/L.[26] In a pooled analysis of 53 mother-infant pairs from published and unpublished cases, the authors found that infants had an average of 2% (range 0 to 15%) of the sertraline plasma concentrations of the mothers’; 3 of the infants had a plasma level greater than 10% of the mothers’, which was considered by the authors as being elevated.[1] Twenty-two breastfed (20 exclusively) infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied. Infant serum levels were measured 2.2 hours (range 0.5 to 5 hours) after nursing. Four infants had detectable sertraline (>2 mcg/L) and 11 infants had detectable norsertraline in their serum with an average concentration of 22 mcg/L. One 11-week-old infant who was being treated for acute asthma with albuterol, inhaled corticosteroids and hydroxyzine had serum levels higher than its mother’s, even though 4 other infants received higher doses of sertraline and norsertraline through milk.[13] In 6 breastfed (extent not stated) infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 15 mg (range 5 to 34 mg), sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<3.4 mcg/L).[14] In a study of mothers given sertraline prophylactically for recurrent postpartum depression, 7 opted to breastfeed. Infant serum was tested at 4 weeks of age with a maternal dosage of 50 mg daily. Sertraline (<2 mcg/L) and norsertraline (<12 mcg/L) were undetectable in the serum of any infant.[27] In a study comparing sertraline to nortriptyline for postpartum depression, 13 infants were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline (dosage and extent of nursing were not stated). After a constant maternal sertraline dosage for at least 14 days, infants had their serum concentrations measured. The infants were an average of 5.9 weeks old at the time of serum sampling. Sertraline was not detectable (<2 mcg/L) in any of the infants’ serum; norsertraline serum levels ranged from undetectable (<2 mcg/L) to 6 mcg/L.[28] At 2 months postpartum, the breastfed infants of 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had undetectable (<0.1 mcg/L) serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline.[15] A 33-week preterm infant was exclusively breastfed by a mother who was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during gestation, at delivery and postpartum. Because of symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence syndrome, the infant’s serum concentrations of sertraline and desmethylsertraline were measured on day 5 postpartum. Levels were 13 and 52 mcg/L, respectively. Because of ongoing symptoms, breastfeeding was stopped on day 9 and the infant’s serum levels reportedly dropped, although specific values were not presented in the paper. The infant was later found to have genetically intermediate metabolism of two of the CYP450 enzymes involved in sertraline metabolism.[16] Authors of a meta-analysis on sertraline reported infant serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline in 25 infants who were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline. Ten of the infants were exclusively breastfed, two were 80% breastfed and the breastfeeding status of the others was not reported. Only two infants, both exclusively breastfed, had detectable serum sertraline levels of 2.1 and 2.4 mcg/L. The other infants had undetectable (<2 mcg/L) sertraline levels. Four other infants had detectable norsertraline levels ranging from 2.6 to 4.7 mcg/L. Sampling times were not reported.[6] Fifteen breastfed (extent not stated) infants with an average age of 1.4 months (range 1.0 to 2.6 months) whose mothers were taking an average sertraline dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) had one blood sample taken for analysis. Their average serum level of sertraline was <2 mcg/L (range <2 to 2.6 mcg/L).[21]

Effects in Breastfed Infants: Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus occurred in one 4-month-old infant and agitation that spontaneously resolved whose mother was taking sertraline 75 mg daily.[25] None of 26 infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily had any detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk. All had been breastfeeding for at least 3 weeks.[13] Whole blood serotonin levels were measured in 14 mothers and their breastfed infants after 6 to 16 weeks of sertraline therapy. Maternal dosages ranged from 25 to 200 mg daily. Although maternal serotonin levels were decreased from 159 mcg/L to 19 mcg/L by sertraline therapy, infant serotonin levels averaged 227 mcg/L before and 224 mcg/L after maternal therapy. The authors concluded that these findings indicate that the amount of sertraline ingested by the infants was not sufficient to affect platelet serotonin uptake in breastfed infants. Platelets and neurons both have the same serotonin transporter, so this lack of effect was seen as indirect evidence of safety of sertraline use during breastfeeding. None of the infants experienced any adverse effects from sertraline in breastmilk, including 6 exclusively breastfed infants under 3 months of age.[29] Twenty-five mothers who took an average sertraline dosage of 82.4 mg daily breastfed their infants exclusively for 4 months and breastfed at least 50% during months 5 and 6. Their infants had 6-month weight gains that were normal according to national growth standards and the mothers reported no abnormal effects in their infants.[30] In 6 infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline 50 to 100 mg daily, no adverse reactions were noted clinically at the time of the study.[14] No adverse effects were seen in 7 infants who were 4 weeks old and whose mothers had been taking sertraline 50 mg daily since day 4 postpartum.[27] One study of side effects of SSRI antidepressants in nursing mothers found no adverse reactions that required medical attention among 2 infants whose mother was taking sertraline. No specific information on maternal sertraline dosage, extent of breastfeeding or infant age was reported.[31] A small study compared the reaction to pain in infants of depressed mothers who had taken an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and nursing, to a control group of unexposed infants of nondepressed mothers. Infants exposed to an SSRI either prenatally alone or prenatally and postnatally via breastmilk had blunted responses to pain compared to control infants. Four of the 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. Because there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, an effect due to maternal behavior caused by depression could not be ruled out. The authors stressed that these findings did not warrant avoiding drug treatment of depression during pregnancy or avoiding breastfeeding during SSRI treatment.[15] An uncontrolled online survey compiled data on 930 mothers who nursed their infants while taking an antidepressant. Infant drug discontinuation symptoms (e.g., irritability, low body temperature, uncontrollable crying, eating and sleeping disorders) were reported in about 10% of infants. Mothers who took antidepressants only during breastfeeding were much less likely to notice symptoms of drug discontinuation in their infants than those who took the drug in pregnancy and lactation.[32] In a telephone follow-up study, 124 mothers who took a benzodiazepine while nursing reported whether their infants had any signs of sedation. One mother who was taking sertraline 50 mg daily, zopiclone 2.5 mg about every 3 days as needed, and also took alprazolam 0.25 mg on 2 occasions, reported sedation in her breastfed infant.[33] A mother was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during gestation, at delivery and postpartum while exclusively breastfeeding her infant. ## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The medication identity was confirmed as **sertraline**. The retrieved LactMed record is lactation-specific; it is not pregnancy evidence.

### Measured exposure

- LactMed describes generally low sertraline concentrations in breast milk. Norsertraline, a weakly active metabolite, was often detectable at low levels in infant serum.
- Across the reported studies, estimated relative infant exposure was generally low, but values varied with milk-sampling methods, timing, breastfeeding extent, and maternal treatment context.
- In one group of 30 breastfed infants aged 6–13 weeks, 22 had undetectable infant serum sertraline; 8 had detectable levels. Other studies reported undetectable sertraline in most or all tested infants, with occasional detectable norsertraline.
- A specific case involved a **33-week preterm infant** with detectable sertraline and norsertraline serum levels and symptoms described as similar to neonatal abstinence. The infant had genetically intermediate metabolism of relevant enzymes. LactMed’s returned text does not provide a complete chronology, and the infant-effects section is truncated.

These are exposure measurements, not by themselves clinical outcomes or proof of causation.

### Observed infant outcomes

- Several small observational groups reported no clinically observed acute adverse effects, and one follow-up group reported normal weight gain through 6 months. These findings come from limited samples; the MCP extract does not establish a complete study count.
- LactMed reports one case of benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in a 4-month-old infant. The returned record does not establish that sertraline caused these findings.
- The preterm-infant case above included symptoms temporally associated with exposure, but the record also describes prematurity and genetically intermediate metabolism; causality is not established.
- LactMed reports no developmental adverse effects in infants followed up to 5 years in the cited material, but this is not a guarantee for every infant or situation.

    "text": "Summary of Use during Lactation: Because of the low levels of sertraline in breastmilk, amounts ingested by the infant are small and is usually not detected in the serum of the infant, although the weakly active metabolite norsertraline (desmethylsertraline) is often detectable in low levels in infant serum. Rarely, preterm infants with impaired metabolic activity might accumulate the drug and demonstrate symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence. No adverse effects on development have been found in infants followed for up to 5 years of age. Most authoritative reviewers consider sertraline a preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.[1-9] Mothers taking an SSRI during pregnancy and postpartum may have more difficulty breastfeeding, although this might be a reflection of their disease state.[10] These mothers may need additional breastfeeding support. Breastfed infants exposed to an SSRI during the third trimester of pregnancy are at risk for neonatal withdrawal syndrome consisting of hypoglycemia, tremors, tachycardia, or hypotonia, and might be at a greater risk of readmission due to jaundice.[11,12]\n\nDrug Levels: Sertraline is metabolized to norsertraline (desmethylsertraline), which has antidepressant activity of about 10% that of sertraline. Maternal Levels. In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 4 unpublished cases, the authors found that 15 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 83 mg (range 25 to 200 mg) had an average breastmilk sertraline level of 45 mcg/L (range 7 to 207 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of sertraline. Twenty-six women who were an average of 15.8 weeks postpartum (range 5 to 36 weeks) and receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied while breastfeeding with extensive milk and serum sampling over a 24-hour period. All milk samples had detectable sertraline (average 129 mcg/L; range 11 to 938 mcg/L) and norsertraline (average 258 mcg/L; range 20 to 1498 mcg/L). Drug concentrations were higher in the hindmilk than the foremilk. Analysis of milk sertraline data from 15 mothers who submitted complete sets of milk samples indicated that the peak concentration of the drug and metabolite occurred 8 to 9 hours after a dose. In these women, the concentration in milk correlated with serum concentration, but not daily dosage. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an average of 0.54% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage and that pumping and discarding milk 8 to 9 hours after the mother’s dose would decrease the infant’s daily dosage by 17%.[13] From data in 6 mothers who were 5 to 34 weeks postpartum and taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 64 mg (range 50 to 100 mg), the authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.9% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[14] At 2 months postpartum, 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had average milk levels of 26.4 mcg/L of sertraline and 29 mcg/L of norsertraline at random times after the previous dose. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.04 mg/kg of sertraline daily.[15] The mother of a preterm infant was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during pregnancy and postpartum. Her breastmilk levels of sertraline and norsertraline on 3 days at random times averaged 201 and 358 mcg/L, respectively.[16] One woman taking sertraline 25 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 29 mcg/L at two times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 4.4 mcg/kg daily or 0.6% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage. In the same paper, 3 women taking sertraline 50 mg daily had an average breastmilk sertraline concentration of 58 mcg/L at times that were not stated. These values equated to an average infant dosage of 8.7 mcg/kg daily or 1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[17] A nursing mother was taking sertraline 50 mg daily. Foremilk and hindmilk samples taken at 4 weeks postpartum, 13 hours after a dose contained 26 mcg/L and 46 mcg/L, respectively.[18] Nine women treated with sertraline 25 to 75 mg daily (7 were taking 50 mg daily) during the third trimester of pregnancy and during breastfeeding provided trough milk samples during the first week postpartum. Sertraline was undetectable (<5 mcg/L) in the milk of 1 woman taking 50 mg daily. In the other 8 women, milk levels ranged from 11.1 to 24.5 mcg/L, with calculated weight-adjusted percentage of maternal dosages ranging from 0.2 to 2.4%. These values might be inaccurate because of the timing of milk sample collection.[19] Random milk samples were obtained from 6 women taking a median dosage of 50 mg (range 25 to 50 mg) of sertraline daily had a median sertraline milk concentration of 11.3 mcg/L (range 3.6 to 35.7 mcg/L). The authors calculated that this represents a median infant dosage of 1.6 (range 0.5 to 5.4) mcg/kg daily. No correlation was found between maternal dosage and milk sertraline level.[20] Fifteen mothers taking sertraline in an average dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) provided milk samples for analysis. Samples of milk from the complete emptying of one breast were collected 3 times over a 2-day period at predefined times between just before a dose and 14 hours after a dose, with each participant collecting samples at different times. The average milk concentration was 87 mcg/L (range 12 to 288 mcg/L) resulting in an average infant daily dosage of 10 mcg/kg and a relative infant dosage of 1%.[21] Thirty-eight mothers taking sertraline with a median daily dose of 50 mg (range 25 to 150 mg) provided 35 blood samples at week 1 postpartum, and 20 at weeks 4 to 6 postpartum. These women also provided 107 breast milk samples, 67 of which were collected at week 1 and 40 at week 4 postpartum. One maternal blood sample was collected and paired with a foremilk and a hindmilk sample. The lower limit of quantification for sertraline was established at 1 mcg/L in plasma and 5 mcg/L in breast milk. These data were used to create a population pharmacokinetic model using NONMEM, which was then used to simulate serum and milk levels in 2000 patients. Simulations suggested a median daily infant dosage of 6.9 mcg/kg with a 50 mg maternal daily dose, representing a relative infant dose of 0.95% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose. The authors found that 100% of simulated infants at maternal doses of 150 mg daily would ingest less than 0.13 mg/kg daily of sertraline, which represents a total of less than 150 mg over 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding.[22] The measurement of fat content in the study may not have been accurate.[23] A woman taking sertraline 100 mg daily provided 5 milk samples between 3.1 and 5.2 days postpartum. Sertraline concentrations ranged from 53.4 mcg/L at 6 hours after a dose to 15.5 mcg/L at 24 hours after a dose.[24] Infant Levels. A paper reported 3 breastfed infants whose mother were taking sertraline. A woman taking 50 mg daily increased her dose to 75 mg daily after 2 weeks. Sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<2 mg/L) in her 4-week-old infant’s serum. Another infant whose mother was taking 75 mg daily which was increased to 100 mg daily had detectable norsertraline (<2 mg/L), but no sertraline (<1 mg/L). A third woman taking 75 mg daily found no detectable sertraline or norsertraline in her infant’s serum at 8 weeks of age. The extent of nursing was not reported in any of the cases.[25] Of 30 breastfed infants (19 exclusively, 11 breastfed 50% or more) aged 6 to 13 weeks, 22 had undetectable (<1 mcg/L) sertraline serum levels during maternal therapy with sertraline dosages of 25 to 200 mg daily. Of the 8 infants who had detectable serum levels, their average sertraline serum level was 7.9 mcg/L. Their mothers, who were taking an average of 109 mg daily, had an average serum level of 52.8 mcg/L.[26] In a pooled analysis of 53 mother-infant pairs from published and unpublished cases, the authors found that infants had an average of 2% (range 0 to 15%) of the sertraline plasma concentrations of the mothers’; 3 of the infants had a plasma level greater than 10% of the mothers’, which was considered by the authors as being elevated.[1] Twenty-two breastfed (20 exclusively) infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied. Infant serum levels were measured 2.2 hours (range 0.5 to 5 hours) after nursing. Four infants had detectable sertraline (>2 mcg/L) and 11 infants had detectable norsertraline in their serum with an average concentration of 22 mcg/L. One 11-week-old infant who was being treated for acute asthma with albuterol, inhaled corticosteroids and hydroxyzine had serum levels higher than its mother’s, even though 4 other infants received higher doses of sertraline and norsertraline through milk.[13] In 6 breastfed (extent not stated) infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline in an average daily dosage of 15 mg (range 5 to 34 mg), sertraline and norsertraline were undetectable (<3.4 mcg/L).[14] In a study of mothers given sertraline prophylactically for recurrent postpartum depression, 7 opted to breastfeed. Infant serum was tested at 4 weeks of age with a maternal dosage of 50 mg daily. Sertraline (<2 mcg/L) and norsertraline (<12 mcg/L) were undetectable in the serum of any infant.[27] In a study comparing sertraline to nortriptyline for postpartum depression, 13 infants were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline (dosage and extent of nursing were not stated). After a constant maternal sertraline dosage for at least 14 days, infants had their serum concentrations measured. The infants were an average of 5.9 weeks old at the time of serum sampling. Sertraline was not detectable (<2 mcg/L) in any of the infants’ serum; norsertraline serum levels ranged from undetectable (<2 mcg/L) to 6 mcg/L.[28] At 2 months postpartum, the breastfed infants of 4 mothers taking an average of 87.5 mg of sertraline daily had undetectable (<0.1 mcg/L) serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline.[15] A 33-week preterm infant was exclusively breastfed by a mother who was taking sertraline 150 mg daily during gestation, at delivery and postpartum. Because of symptoms similar to neonatal abstinence syndrome, the infant’s serum concentrations of sertraline and desmethylsertraline were measured on day 5 postpartum. Levels were 13 and 52 mcg/L, respectively. Because of ongoing symptoms, breastfeeding was stopped on day 9 and the infant’s serum levels reportedly dropped, although specific values were not presented in the paper. The infant was later found to have genetically intermediate metabolism of two of the CYP450 enzymes involved in sertraline metabolism.[16] Authors of a meta-analysis on sertraline reported infant serum levels of sertraline and norsertraline in 25 infants who were breastfed by mothers taking sertraline. Ten of the infants were exclusively breastfed, two were 80% breastfed and the breastfeeding status of the others was not reported. Only two infants, both exclusively breastfed, had detectable serum sertraline levels of 2.1 and 2.4 mcg/L. The other infants had undetectable (<2 mcg/L) sertraline levels. Four other infants had detectable norsertraline levels ranging from 2.6 to 4.7 mcg/L. Sampling times were not reported.[6] Fifteen breastfed (extent not stated) infants with an average age of 1.4 months (range 1.0 to 2.6 months) whose mothers were taking an average sertraline dosage of 83 mg daily (range 50 to 200 mg daily) had one blood sample taken for analysis. Their average serum level of sertraline was <2 mcg/L (range <2 to 2.6 mcg/L).[21]\n\nEffects in Breastfed Infants: Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus occurred in one 4-month-old infant and agitation that spontaneously resolved whose mother was taking sertraline 75 mg daily.[25] None of 26 infants with an average age of 16.6 weeks (range 4 to 28 weeks) whose mothers were receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily had any detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breastmilk. All had been breastfeeding for at least 3 weeks.[13] Whole blood serotonin levels were measured in 14 mothers and their breastfed infants after 6 to 16 weeks of sertraline therapy. Maternal dosages ranged from 25 to 200 mg daily. Although maternal serotonin levels were decreased from 159 mcg/L to 19 mcg/L by sertraline therapy, infant serotonin levels averaged 227 mcg/L before and 224 mcg/L after maternal therapy. The authors concluded that these findings indicate that the amount of sertraline ingested by the infants was not sufficient to affect platelet serotonin uptake in breastfed infants. Platelets and neurons both have the same serotonin transporter, so this lack of effect was seen as indirect evidence of safety of sertraline use during breastfeeding. None of the infants experienced any adverse effects from sertraline in breastmilk, including 6 exclusively breastfed infants under 3 months of age.[29] Twenty-five mothers who took an average sertraline dosage of 82.4 mg daily breastfed their infants exclusively for 4 months and breastfed at least 50% during months 5 and 6. Their infants had 6-month weight gains that were normal according to national growth standards and the mothers reported no abnormal effects in their infants.[30] In 6 infants aged 5 to 34 weeks whose mothers were taking sertraline 50 to 100 mg daily, no adverse reactions were noted clinically at the time of the study.[14] No adverse effects were seen in 7 infants who were 4 weeks old and whose mothers had been taking sertraline 50 mg daily since day 4 postpartum.[27] One study of side effects of SSRI antidepressants in nursing mothers found no adverse reactions that required medical attention among 2 infants whose mother was taking sertraline. No specific information on maternal sertraline dosage, extent of breastfeeding or infant age was reported.[31] A small study compared the reaction to pain in infants of depressed mothers who had taken an SSRI during pregnancy alone or during pregnancy and nursing, to a control group of unexposed infants of nondepressed mothers. Infants exposed to an SSRI either prenatally alone or prenatally and postnatally via breastmilk had blunted responses to pain compared to control infants. Four of the 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. Because there was no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers, an effect due to maternal behavior caused by depression could not be ruled out. The authors stressed that these findings did not warrant avoiding drug treatment of depression during pregnancy or avoiding breastfeeding during SSRI treatment.[15] An uncontrolled online survey compiled data on 930 mothers who nursed their infants while taking an antidepressant. Infant drug discontinuation symptoms (e.g., irritability, low body temperature, uncontrollable crying, eating and sleeping disorders) were reported in about 10% of infants. Mothers who took antidepressants only during breastfeeding were much less likely to notice symptoms of drug discontinuation in their infants than those who took the drug in pregnancy and lactation.[32] In a telephone follow-up study, 124 mothers who took a benzodiazepine while nursing reported whether their infants had any signs of sedation. ## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The retrieved record confirms the ingredient as **sertraline**. LactMed is lactation-specific and does not provide pregnancy evidence. [S9](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Measured milk and infant exposure

- LactMed reports generally low sertraline concentrations in breast milk. The metabolite **norsertraline** was often detectable at low levels in infant serum. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In reported studies, infant serum sertraline was frequently undetectable, although some infants had measurable sertraline and/or norsertraline. Exposure estimates varied with sampling timing, breastfeeding extent, and study population. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One report involved a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks** with measured sertraline and norsertraline in serum. The record also describes genetically intermediate metabolism; the retrieved evidence does not establish that sertraline caused the reported symptoms. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are measured exposure findings, not clinical outcomes by themselves.

### Observed infant outcomes

- Several small observational groups reported no observed acute adverse effects, and one group reported normal infant weight gain through 6 months. The retrieved LactMed metadata does not establish a study count; missing study counts are unknown, not zero. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed reports one 4-month-old infant with benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation. The source does not establish causation. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In the preterm-infant report, symptoms described as similar to neonatal abstinence occurred in the context of prematurity and genetically intermediate metabolism. The returned extract is insufficient to determine the causal contribution of sertraline. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed’s summary reports no developmental adverse effects in infants followed for up to 5 years in the cited material, but this does not establish safety for every infant or circumstance. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Completeness limitation:** The retrieved LactMed “Effects in Breastfed Infants” section is truncated, and “Effects on Lactation and Breastmilk” was omitted by the retrieval limit. This is not a complete LactMed record. [S10](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
